items.topic: sampling-t2 · unbiasedness and variance of stratified and simple-random-sampling means
items.stem: A population of size N is divided into L strata of sizes N₁,…,N_L. A stratified random sample of size n is drawn, with n_j units selected by simple random sampling within stratum j. Let ȳ_j be the sample mean in stratum j and define ȳ_st=∑_{j=1}^L(N_j/N)ȳ_j. An independent simple random sample of size n is also drawn from the population, with sample mean ȳ and variance of the sample mean σ². Which statements are correct?
statements: ȳ_st is an unbiased estimator of the population mean.
ȳ is an unbiased estimator of the population mean.
The variance σ²_st of ȳ_st is always less than or equal to σ².
If n_j/N_j=n/N for every stratum j, then σ²_st=σ².

A.why: Each stratum sample mean is design-unbiased for its stratum population mean, so their population-weighted sum is unbiased. The ordinary SRS sample mean is also unbiased.

B.why: Under simple random sampling, the sample mean is design-unbiased for the population mean.

C.why: Proportional allocation does not generally make the two variances equal. The stratified variance depends on within-stratum variation, while SRS variance also reflects between-stratum variation.

D.why: Statements 3 and 4 are not universal identities; proportional allocation alone does not imply equal variances.

items.explanation: For each stratum j, simple random sampling within that stratum gives E(ȳ_j)=Ȳ_j, the stratum population mean. Therefore E(ȳ_st)=∑(N_j/N)Ȳ_j=Ȳ, so statement 1 is true. An ordinary simple random sample mean is also unbiased for the population mean, so statement 2 is true. The variance of a stratified estimator is not always smaller than the SRS variance: the allocation across strata matters, and an inefficient allocation can increase variance. Thus statement 3 is false as a universal claim. Under proportional allocation, n_j/N_j=n/N, the variance expression still involves the within-stratum variances. The SRS variance involves the overall population variance, which includes both within- and between-stratum components. They are not generally equal, so statement 4 is false. Hence only statements 1 and 2 are correct. Other-exam relevance: stratified sampling, unbiasedness and design variance are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi; This is topic overlap, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those other examinations.

items.topic: sampling-t10 · simple random sampling with and without replacement; unbiasedness and finite-population correction
items.stem: A sample of size n is drawn from a finite population of N households, where 1<n<N (editorial clarification; the source scan states only 0<n<N), to estimate the proportion of households with more than one earning member. Sample I is selected by simple random sampling without replacement, and Sample II by simple random sampling with replacement. Let p₁ and p₂ be the respective sample proportions, and let σᵢ²=Var(pᵢ), i=1,2. Which statements are true?
statements: p₁ is unbiased for the population proportion, but p₂ is not.
p₂ is unbiased for the population proportion, but p₁ is not.
σ₁²<σ₂².
σ₂²<σ₁².

A.why: Both sample proportions are unbiased for the population proportion under their respective simple random sampling designs.

B.why: Sampling with replacement does not introduce bias in the sample proportion; both estimators are unbiased.

C.why: For 0<n<N, sampling without replacement has the finite-population correction (N−n)/(N−1), reducing the variance relative to sampling with replacement.

D.why: The variance ordering is the reverse: without-replacement sampling has lower variance for the sample proportion.

items.explanation: Let P be the fixed population proportion. Under either design, each draw or selected unit has expectation P, so both sample proportions are unbiased; statements 1 and 2 are false. Under SRSWR, the draws are independent Bernoulli(P), giving Var(p₂)=P(1−P)/n. Under SRSWOR, Var(p₁)=P(1−P)/n × (N−n)/(N−1). For 1<n<N, this finite-population correction is strictly below one, so statement 3 is true. Important boundary note: when n=1, the correction equals one and the two variances are equal. The source scan states only 0<n<N, which includes n=1 and makes the strict inequality false at that boundary. To make this scored practice version mathematically valid, the stem has been editorially clarified to 1<n<N; this added restriction is not present in the original CSIR question. The printed answer key identifies statement 3 as the intended answer. Other-exam relevance: simple random sampling, finite-population correction and variance comparison are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is topic overlap, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those other examinations.

items.topic: sampling-t5 · circular systematic sampling; unbiasedness of the sample mean and bias of the usual sample variance
items.stem: For circular systematic sampling, which of the following statements are correct?
statements: The sample mean is an unbiased estimator of the population mean, but the usual sample variance is not an unbiased estimator of the population variance.
The sample mean and the usual sample variance are unbiased estimators of the population mean and population variance, respectively.
The sample mean is not an unbiased estimator of the population mean, but the usual sample variance is an unbiased estimator of the population variance.
Neither the sample mean nor the usual sample variance is an unbiased estimator of its population counterpart.

A.why: Circular systematic sampling gives every population unit the same first-order inclusion probability, so the design expectation of the sample mean is the population mean. The usual within-sample variance does not, in general, estimate the population variance without bias.

B.why: The sample mean is unbiased, but the usual sample variance is not generally unbiased under this design.

C.why: The sample mean is design-unbiased because each unit has the same chance of appearing in the sample.

D.why: The sample mean is unbiased, so it is incorrect to say that neither estimator is unbiased.

items.explanation: The answer key on page 63 of the supplied Estimation CSIR NET PDF gives Question 37 as statement 1. We can understand the two parts separately. First, circular systematic sampling chooses a random start and then selects units at a fixed interval around the ordered population. Every population unit has the same first-order inclusion probability. Therefore, when we average the sample mean over all possible random starts, each population value receives the same weight, and the expected sample mean equals the population mean. So the sample mean is unbiased. Second, the usual sample variance is calculated only from the units that appear together in the realised systematic sample. Systematic samples do not contain all possible combinations of units; many pairs have zero probability of appearing together. As a result, the usual sample variance does not, in general, average to the population variance over the design. Thus statement 1 alone is correct, option A. Remember: an estimator can be unbiased for the mean even when the familiar sample-variance formula is not an unbiased estimator of population variance under that sampling design. Other-exam relevance: systematic sampling, inclusion probabilities and design-based unbiasedness are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: sampling-t10 · simple random sampling without replacement; unbiased estimation of P(1−P) and finite-population correction
items.stem: A simple random sample of size n is drawn without replacement from a finite population of size N, where 1<n<N. Let P be the population proportion with a specified attribute and p the corresponding sample proportion. Which expression is an unbiased estimator of P(1−P)?
items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 55 (December 2017) on page 28. The supplied answer list on page 63 ends at Question 44, so no printed key is available; the result follows from the SRSWOR variance formula. The sample proportion is unbiased: E(p)=P. Also Var(p)=[(N−n)/(N−1)]·P(1−P)/n. Since p(1−p)=p−p², take expectations: E[p(1−p)]=E(p)−E(p²)=P−{Var(p)+[E(p)]²}=P−Var(p)−P²=P(1−P)−Var(p). Substitute the variance: E[p(1−p)]=P(1−P)[1−(N−n)/(n(N−1))]. Simplifying the bracket gives N(n−1)/[n(N−1)]. Therefore multiplying p(1−p) by the reciprocal n(N−1)/[N(n−1)] produces an unbiased estimator of P(1−P). This is option C. Other-exam relevance: SRSWOR, finite-population correction, sample proportions and unbiased estimation are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations. Printed answer-key cross-check (source PDF page 64): Q55 is listed as C.

items.topic: sampling-t6 · PPS sampling with replacement, inclusion probabilities and Hansen–Hurwitz estimation
items.stem: A sample of size 2 is drawn with replacement from four population units using probabilities p₁=0.2, p₂=0.3, p₃=0.1 and p₄=0.4. Let πᵢ and πᵢⱼ be first- and second-order inclusion probabilities. Which statements are correct?
statements: T=(1/2)Σ(yᵢ/pᵢ), summed over the two draws and counting repeats, is unbiased for the population total.
π₁+π₂+π₃+π₄=2.

A.why: Each draw's yᵢ/pᵢ has expectation Σyᵢ, so the average over two draws is unbiased for the total.

C.why: Both units 1 and 2 appear in two draws only for ordered outcomes (1,2) or (2,1), so π₁₂=2p₁p₂=0.12.

D.why: The sum of inclusion probabilities is the expected number of distinct sampled units, which is below 2 when repeats are possible.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 69 (June 2016), page 36. No printed answer-key entry is available. For each draw, the Hansen–Hurwitz contribution yᵢ/pᵢ has expectation Σpᵢ(yᵢ/pᵢ)=Σyᵢ, the population total. Averaging the two contributions remains unbiased, so A is true. The probability that unit i appears at least once is πᵢ=1−(1−pᵢ)². Hence π₁=1−0.8²=0.36 and π₂=1−0.7²=0.51, proving B. Both units 1 and 2 appear only for ordered outcomes (1,2) or (2,1), so π₁₂=2(0.2)(0.3)=0.12, proving C. The sum of inclusion probabilities is the expected number of distinct units selected; numerically it is 0.36+0.51+0.19+0.64=1.70, not 2. D is false. Correct combination A, B and C only, option A. Other-exam relevance: PPS sampling, inclusion probabilities and Hansen–Hurwitz estimation overlap with UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations. Printed answer-key cross-check (source PDF page 64): Q69 is listed as A,B,C.

items.topic: sampling-t6 · Hansen–Hurwitz estimation and variance estimation under PPS with replacement
items.stem: A finite population has N units with values yᵢ and total Y=Σyᵢ. Draw n>1 units independently with replacement using probabilities pᵢ, Σpᵢ=1, and let T=(1/n)Σ(yᵢ/pᵢ), summed over draws. Which statements are true?
statements: T is unbiased for the population mean Y/N.
T is unbiased for the population total Y.
Var(T)=0 if yᵢ is proportional to pᵢ for every i.
An unbiased estimator of Var(T) is [1/{n(n−1)}]Σ(yᵢ/pᵢ−T)², summed over draws.

A.why: T is scaled to estimate the total; divide by N to estimate the population mean.

B.why: Each draw's yᵢ/pᵢ has expectation Σyᵢ=Y, so their average is unbiased for Y.

C.why: If yᵢ=cpᵢ, every draw contributes the same constant c, so T has zero variance.

D.why: The sample variance of the draw contributions divided by n is unbiased for the variance of their sample mean.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 76 (December 2015), page 40. No printed answer-key entry is available. Let Zⱼ be yᵢ/pᵢ for draw j. E(Zⱼ)=Σpᵢ(yᵢ/pᵢ)=Y, so T=Z̄ is unbiased for the total, not the mean; B is true and A false. If yᵢ=cpᵢ for all units, every Zⱼ=c, so T is constant and C is true. The sample variance s²_Z=(1/(n−1))Σ(Zⱼ−Z̄)² is unbiased for Var(Zⱼ). Since Var(T)=Var(Zⱼ)/n, s²_Z/n=[1/{n(n−1)}]Σ(Zⱼ−T)² is unbiased for Var(T), so D is true. Correct combination B, C and D only, option B. Other-exam relevance: PPS with replacement, Hansen–Hurwitz estimation and variance estimation overlap with UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations. Printed answer-key cross-check (source PDF page 64): Q76 is listed as B,C,D.

items.topic: sampling-t2 · stratified sampling with equal stratum sizes and unequal allocation
items.stem: A population has k strata of equal size M. Draw nᵢ units with replacement from stratum i. Let ȳᵢ be the sample mean, ȳ_s=(1/k)Σȳᵢ and ȳ_w=Σnᵢȳᵢ/n. Which statement is necessarily true?
options: ȳ_s is unbiased but ȳ_w is not necessarily unbiased for the population mean.
ȳ_s is not unbiased but ȳ_w is unbiased for the population mean.
Both ȳ_s and ȳ_w are unbiased for the population mean.
Neither ȳ_s nor ȳ_w is unbiased for the population mean.
items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 78 (June 2015), page 41. No printed answer-key entry is available. Since each stratum has the same population size, the population mean is Ȳ=(1/k)ΣȲᵢ. Each sample mean ȳᵢ is unbiased for its stratum mean, so E(ȳ_s)=(1/k)ΣE(ȳᵢ)=Ȳ. The weighted estimator ȳ_w uses weights nᵢ/n, which need not equal 1/k. Its expectation is Σ(nᵢ/n)Ȳᵢ, not generally the equal-stratum population mean unless allocation is equal or the stratum means happen to be equal. Thus option A is necessarily true. Other-exam relevance: stratified sampling, allocation and design-unbiased estimation overlap with UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations. Printed answer-key cross-check (source PDF page 64): Q78 is listed as A.

items.topic: sampling-t10 · SRSWOR estimation of a finite-population total with one known unit
items.stem: An SRSWOR sample of size n is drawn from N population units. Let ȳ be its sample mean. If one population value y₁ is known, draw an SRSWOR sample of size n from the remaining N−1 units and let ȳ₀ be its sample mean. Define t₁=Nȳ and t₂=(N−1)ȳ₀+y₁. Which statements are necessarily true?
statements: t₁ is unbiased for the population total.
t₂ is unbiased for the population total.
Var(t₁)=N²σ²(N−n)/[n(N−1)], where σ² is the finite-population variance.
Var(t₂)≤Var(t₁) for every population and all n,N.

B.why: The known unit contributes y₁ exactly and (N−1)ȳ₀ is unbiased for the remaining population total.

C.why: This is the standard SRSWOR variance formula for the estimated total Nȳ.

D.why: Using the finite-population variance relation after removing a known unit and the SRSWOR variance formula for the remaining N−1 units gives Var(t₂)≤Var(t₁).

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 81 (June 2015), page 43. The supplied answer key on page 64 lists A, B, C and D. Under SRSWOR, E(ȳ)=Y/N, so t₁=Nȳ is unbiased for the total. For t₂, y₁ is known exactly and ȳ₀ is unbiased for the mean of the remaining N−1 units; hence t₂ is also unbiased. The standard SRSWOR variance formula gives Var(t₁)=N²σ²(N−n)/[n(N−1)]. For t₂, the variance among the remaining N−1 units is bounded above by N/(N−1) times the original finite-population variance. Substituting this bound into the SRSWOR variance formula for the remaining population gives Var(t₂)≤Var(t₁). Therefore all four statements are true, option D. Other-exam relevance: SRSWOR, finite-population corrections and estimation of population totals overlap with UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations. Printed answer-key cross-check (source PDF page 64): Q81 is listed as A,B,C,D.

items.topic: sampling-t10 · hypergeometric likelihood and estimation of an unknown finite population size
items.stem: A population has N units, of which m=40 are marked. A simple random sample of n=30 units is drawn without replacement, and x=10 marked units are observed. Treat N as unknown. What is the maximum-likelihood estimate of N?
items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 104 (June 2011), page 57. No printed answer-key entry is available. The likelihood, ignoring factors that do not depend on N, is L(N)∝C(N−40,20)/C(N,30), with N≥60. Compare successive integer values using the ratio L(N+1)/L(N)=[(N−39)(N−29)]/[(N−59)(N+1)]. This ratio is greater than 1 for N<119, equals 1 at N=119, and is less than 1 for N>119. Therefore the likelihood increases up to N=119, has equal values at N=119 and N=120, and then decreases. There are two maximisers, so the MLE is not unique. Option D is correct. Other-exam relevance: hypergeometric sampling, likelihoods for finite-population parameters and MLEs for discrete parameters overlap with UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations. The supplied answer key on page 65 lists option A (N=75), but the likelihood ratio calculation gives equal maxima at N=119 and N=120, both larger than the likelihood at N=75. The bank retains the mathematically derived non-unique MLE and flags the key discrepancy. Printed answer-key cross-check (source PDF page 65): Q104 is listed as A.
